items.content:
Cracks in the US private credit industry are widening:

Loans marked as non-accrual across the 20 largest publicly traded business development companies (BDCs) rose +0.8 percentage points in Q2 2026, to a median 2.8% of cost, the highest since 2017.

BDCs are publicly traded firms that lend to small, mid-sized, and distressed US businesses, giving retail investors access to private credit markets.

This increase means a growing share of private-credit borrowers have either stopped making payments or are at risk of defaulting on their loans.

Furthermore, new funding commitments minus the value of investments repaid or sold across the 12 largest listed BDCs fell to -$2.5 billion in Q2 2025, the lowest in at least 2.5 years.

This marks the 3rd consecutive quarter of negative net funding.

Meanwhile, Fitch Ratings said last week that private credit defaults rose to an all-time high in July.

Stress in the $2 trillion private credit market is intensifying.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Aug 21, 2026

items.title: US hiring is showing signs of a recovery: 20% of small business owners said in July that they plan to hire over the next 3 months, the highest since October 2022. By comparison, the average since the 1970s is just ~11%. This also marks a +9 percentage point MoM increase, the largest monthly improvement in hiring intentions on record. This even surpasses the sharp recovery seen following the 2020 pandemic drop. Historically, this indicator has led nonfarm private payrolls by 3-6 months, as small firms account for ~46% of all US private sector employment. If history holds, a stronger jobs report could be just months away.

items.title: US stocks are having one of their best decades in history: The S&P 500 has gained +141.0% so far since the end of 2019. If this pace continues, the index will finish the decade with a cumulative gain of roughly +277%. This would rank as the 2nd-best decade on record, trailing only the +316% return posted during the 1989-1999 Dot-Com Boom. This would also surpass the +257% gain seen during the postwar boom decade of 1949-1959. By comparison, between 2010 and 2020, the S&P 500 returned +190% following the 2008 Financial Crisis. The 2020s are shaping up to be one of the greatest decades in US equity market history.
